tools.keywords: salary hourly wage pay rate annual income per hour convert
tools.title_tag: Salary to Hourly Calculator – Pay per Hour, Free
tools.meta: Turn a yearly salary into an hourly, daily, weekly and monthly figure using the hours you actually work. Arithmetic only, no tax rules.
tools.lede: Enter a yearly salary plus the hours and weeks you work, and the tool divides it down to an hourly rate with the daily, weekly and monthly equivalents.
tools.how: The hourly rate is the yearly salary divided by the paid hours in a year, and those hours are your hours per week multiplied by your weeks per year. Forty hours over fifty-two weeks is 2,080 hours, so a 52,000 salary gives 25.00 an hour. The weekly figure divides the salary by the number of weeks, the monthly figure divides it by twelve, and the daily figure takes the hourly rate and multiplies it by the weekly hours divided by five. Every result is printed with the arithmetic that produced it, so you can check each line yourself. No tax, pension or holiday rules are applied: the tool only divides the number you type.
tools.example: For a 52,000 salary at 40 hours a week over 52 weeks, the paid hours are 40 × 52 = 2,080. The hourly rate is 52,000 ÷ 2,080 = 25.00. The daily figure is 25.00 × (40 ÷ 5) = 200.00, the weekly figure is 52,000 ÷ 52 = 1,000.00, and the monthly figure is 52,000 ÷ 12 = 4,333.33.

faq.q: Does this include tax?
faq.a: No. It is arithmetic only: no income tax, national insurance, pension or student loan is subtracted. Type the gross salary to compare job offers, or a net figure if you already know your take-home pay.

faq.q: Why divide by hours per week times weeks per year?
faq.a: Because that product is the number of paid hours in a year. At 40 hours over 52 weeks it is 2,080 hours, so dividing the salary by 2,080 gives the rate for each paid hour.

faq.q: Should I use 52 weeks if I get paid holiday?
faq.a: Use the number of weeks you are actually paid for. If your salary is spread across the full year including holiday, keep 52. If you are paid only for weeks worked, enter the smaller number.

faq.q: How is the daily figure worked out?
faq.a: The hourly rate is multiplied by your weekly hours divided by five. That assumes five working days sharing the same weekly hours, so it is an average, not a timesheet.

faq.q: What if my hours change from week to week?
faq.a: Enter an average week. The result is a straight division, so it can only be as accurate as that average.

tools.keywords: keyword density word frequency counter repetition percentage text
tools.title_tag: Keyword Density Analyzer – Word Counts, Free
tools.meta: Paste text to see how often each word appears, with counts and percentages from a stated formula. Up to 50,000 characters, nothing uploaded.
tools.lede: Paste an article or a page of copy to see which words repeat and what share of the text each one takes, with the formula printed beside the result.
tools.how: The text is split into words: runs of letters and digits, keeping apostrophes and hyphens that sit inside a word, so "don't" counts once. Every word is lowercased, then counted. Density for a word is its count divided by the total number of words, multiplied by one hundred, and that number is what the percentage column shows. Ties are listed alphabetically. Ticking the option to ignore common words removes a built-in list of function words such as "the" and "and" from both the count and the total, so the percentages then describe only the remaining words. The input is capped at 50,000 characters and 20,000 words, and the twelve most frequent words are shown.
tools.example: For "The cat sat on the mat. The cat slept." the tool reads nine words: the, cat, sat, on, the, mat, the, cat and slept. "the" appears three times, so its density is 3 ÷ 9 × 100 = 33.33%. "cat" appears twice, so 2 ÷ 9 × 100 = 22.22%. The four remaining words appear once each, which is 11.11% each, and there are six different words in total.

faq.q: What counts as a word here?
faq.a: A run of letters and digits. Apostrophes and hyphens are kept when they sit between characters, so "don't" and "e-mail" each count once. Punctuation on its own is ignored.

faq.q: Why do the percentages change when I ignore common words?
faq.a: The option removes the stop words from both the count and the total, so the percentages are recalculated over the remaining words. They will not add up to the same totals as the full text.

faq.q: Does keyword density affect search rankings?
faq.a: This tool does not measure a ranking effect and makes no such claim. It reports how often words repeat in the text you paste, which is all the numbers measure.

faq.q: Is my text uploaded anywhere?
faq.a: No. The counting runs in the page with JavaScript. Nothing is sent, stored or written to a cookie.

faq.q: How many words are listed?
faq.a: The twelve most frequent, highest first, with ties in alphabetical order. The totals above the list cover the whole input, not just those twelve.

tools.keywords: meta tags title description open graph twitter card canonical html head seo
tools.title_tag: Meta Tag Generator – Title, OG and Twitter
tools.meta: Build a title, description, canonical, Open Graph and Twitter card block as plain text, with length counters as you type. Nothing is uploaded.
tools.lede: Fill in the page details and copy a ready block of head tags, with a live character count for the title and the description.
tools.how: The tool assembles the tags in a fixed order: the title element, the description, the canonical link, the Open Graph tags, then the Twitter card tags. Open Graph and Twitter tags repeat the title, description and image under different attribute names because each service reads a different set. Attribute values are escaped, so an ampersand becomes & and a double quote becomes ", which keeps the block valid HTML. The two counters show the title and description lengths against 60 and 160 characters, the usual display lengths in search results; going over them is allowed but may be truncated. Optional fields are skipped when left empty, so a page with no image simply gets no image tags. Everything is produced in the browser as text.
tools.example: With the title "Blue mug — Stacklane" (20 characters), the description "A 350 ml ceramic mug." (21 characters), the URL https://YOURDOMAIN.com/mug.html, the image https://YOURDOMAIN.com/mug.png and the site name Stacklane, the tool prints thirteen lines. The first three are <title>Blue mug — Stacklane</title>, then <meta name="description" content="A 350 ml ceramic mug.">, then <link rel="canonical" href="https://YOURDOMAIN.com/mug.html">. The block ends with the Twitter card and image tags for the same page.

faq.q: Where do these tags go?
faq.a: Inside the head element of the page, before the closing </head>. Paste the whole block as it is.

faq.q: Will this improve my ranking?
faq.a: No claim is made about rankings. A title and description are what a search engine may show for the page, and whether it uses them is its decision, not something this tool can guarantee.

faq.q: Why is twitter:card always summary_large_image?
faq.a: Because it tells the service to use a wide image. If your image is small or square, change that value to "summary" by hand after pasting.

faq.q: Are the 60 and 160 counters hard limits?
faq.a: They are the lengths usually shown in results before truncation, not limits on what HTML accepts. Text over them is valid; it may simply be cut off in a preview.

faq.q: Does the generator escape special characters?
faq.a: Yes. Ampersands, angle brackets and double quotes in your text are written as entities, so a title containing an ampersand still produces valid HTML.

tools.keywords: robots txt generator crawler allow disallow sitemap crawl rules
tools.meta: Write a robots.txt in plain text: allow everything, block everything or list your own paths, then add a sitemap line. Free, in your browser.
tools.lede: Choose what crawlers may fetch, list any paths of your own, and copy a finished robots.txt with each directive explained.
tools.how: The file is built from directives, one per line. User-agent names the crawler the following rules apply to, and an asterisk means all of them. Disallow lists paths that must not be fetched, and an empty Disallow means nothing is blocked, which is how a file allows everything. A line starting with a bang in the paths box becomes an Allow line instead, so you can block a folder and reopen one file inside it. Blank lines separate groups and are ignored. The optional Sitemap line takes a full URL and points crawlers at the sitemap; it is not part of any group. Paths must start with a slash. The output is plain text you can copy or download as robots.txt.
tools.example: With "allow everything" selected and the sitemap https://YOURDOMAIN.com/sitemap.xml, the tool writes three lines: User-agent: * then Disallow: with nothing after it, then a blank line and Sitemap: https://YOURDOMAIN.com/sitemap.xml. The empty Disallow is deliberate: it means no path is blocked, which is the usual way to say everything is allowed.

faq.q: Does robots.txt remove a page from search results?
faq.a: Not reliably. It asks crawlers not to fetch a URL, but a blocked page can still appear in results if other sites link to it. To keep a page out of results, let it be crawled and send a noindex robots meta tag instead.

faq.q: Where does robots.txt have to live?
faq.a: At the root of the domain, so the address is https://YOURDOMAIN.com/robots.txt. A copy in a subfolder is not read for that domain.

faq.q: What does an empty Disallow line mean?
faq.a: Nothing is disallowed, so every path may be fetched. That is the standard way to allow a whole site while still naming the user agent.

faq.q: Can I block a folder but allow one file inside it?
faq.a: Yes, in custom mode. Add a line for the folder and prefix the file's line with an exclamation mark to make it an Allow rule; most crawlers then use the longest matching rule.

faq.q: Do all crawlers follow these rules?
faq.a: Most well-known search crawlers do. Any crawler is free to ignore the file, so it is a request rather than a lock.

tools.keywords: xml sitemap generator urls crawl seo loc urlset changefreq priority
tools.title_tag: XML Sitemap Generator – Paste URLs, Get XML
tools.meta: Paste page URLs to get a valid sitemap.xml: escaped characters, duplicates removed, and your chosen change frequency and priority.
tools.lede: Paste one URL per line and the tool writes a complete sitemap XML file, escaping special characters and dropping duplicates on the way.
tools.how: Each non-empty line is checked as a URL that starts with http or https and contains a domain. Lines that fail are reported with the text that caused the problem, and duplicates are removed with a count. The surviving URLs are written as url entries inside a urlset element, each with a loc element, the change frequency you picked and the priority you picked. Five characters are escaped as XML entities: ampersands, angle brackets, double quotes and apostrophes, because an unescaped ampersand makes the file invalid. The result is capped at 5,000 URLs. You can copy it or download it as sitemap.xml. The file is assembled in the browser and nothing is uploaded.
tools.example: Pasting https://YOURDOMAIN.com/ and https://YOURDOMAIN.com/list.html?tag=a&sort=2 with monthly frequency and priority 0.7 produces a file that starts with the XML declaration and the urlset element, then two url blocks. In the second block the loc line reads https://YOURDOMAIN.com/list.html?tag=a&sort=2, because the ampersand must be escaped for the XML to be valid. The file closes with the urlset end tag.

faq.q: What is a sitemap actually for?
faq.a: It is a list of URLs you want crawlers to know about. It helps them find pages, but it does not guarantee that a page is crawled, indexed or ranked.

faq.q: Why is the ampersand replaced with &?
faq.a: XML reserves the ampersand, so a raw one makes the document invalid and a parser will reject it. Writing & is the correct way to include an ampersand in a URL inside XML.

faq.q: How many URLs can I add?
faq.a: This page accepts 5,000. The sitemap format itself allows up to 50,000 URLs and 50 MB per file, beyond which you split into several files and an index.

faq.q: Do changefreq and priority matter?
faq.a: They are hints. Google says it ignores both; other search engines may differ. The file is still useful without them, so keep the values honest rather than optimistic.

faq.q: Where should the file go?
faq.a: At the site root as sitemap.xml, and reference it in robots.txt with a Sitemap line so crawlers can find it.
